name: Biseni
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The dialect names are abbreviated as follows: OR = Oruma ... BI = Biseni KO = Kolokuma ... OA = Okordia [...] In terms of the usual typology, dialects 11-12, 312-319 would be classified as two-level tone systems without downstep, dialects 13-311 as two-level tone systems with downstep, and dialects 321-42 as pitch-accent systems. [...] The pitch pattern of a group is chiefly, in many cases entirely, determined by the class of the initial morpheme ... Thus a group can be conceived as having a prosodic structure in which the first morpheme is strong and the others weak.
new_statements.citation: Williamson, Kay. 1988. Tone and accent in Ijo. In Harry van der Hulst & Norval Smith (eds.), Autosegmental Studies on Pitch Accent (Linguistic Models 11), 253-278. Dordrecht: Foris.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.1, p. 253 (dialect codes in fn. 1: '12 BI = Biseni'; Table 1 p. 254, Table 2 p. 255); sec. 1.2 item 3, p. 255

new_statements.rule_in_words: Biseni (Williamson's dialect 12, with Oruma = 11) is classed as a two-level (H/L) tone language without downstep; morphemes belong to lexical tone classes, and within a syntactically defined tone 'group' the initial morpheme determines the pitch pattern of the whole group. No word stress is described; the only prominence notion is the group-initial 'strong' morpheme.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial V-syllables sometimes pattern differently from initial CV-syllables (Table 1 note); otherwise none for Biseni. Note the later encyclopedia summary by Williamson & Blench (2006/2009) says 'inland Ijo ha[s] two tones plus downstep', which disagrees with the 1988 no-downstep grouping for Biseni/Oruma (Okordia = 13 is in the downstep group in 1988).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the lexical/pitch system type (isolation forms of morphemes in Table 1) and the phrase-level 'group' (object+verb, noun+modifiers) whose first morpheme is prosodically strong; Biseni enters only as one row of a 28-dialect comparative table, not as the object of a dedicated description. Text verified only through archive.org scanned search fragments of a controlled-lending scan; dialect-number strings (11-12, 13-311, 321-42) are scanned and should be checked against print.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1988 treats Biseni as dialect '12 BI' of her language 1 (Inland Ijo: 11 Oruma, 12 Biseni, 13 Okordia) within a 28-dialect Ijo comparison; the statement groups Biseni with Oruma [orum1241?/Oruma] as no-downstep two-tone systems and separates Okordia (okod1238, downstep). Older literature calls the lect Amegi or Amegi-Biseni (Williamson 1965) and Ethnologue once listed it as 'Ijo, Northeast Central'. The Williamson & Blench encyclopedia line is about 'inland Ijo' as a group (Biseni + Akita/Okordia + Tugbeni/Oruma), not Biseni alone.
